description: How Allied victory and Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe set the terms of the Cold War.
content_html:
From Alliance to Antagonism

In 1941, Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union found themselves allied against Nazi Germany. By 1947–48, those same partners had hardened into opposing camps, dividing Europe along ideological lines that would define international relations for the next four decades. Understanding how that transformation happened requires examining two key wartime conferences, the decisions made in their aftermath, and the competing perspectives historians have offered about responsibility for the breakdown.

Key Fact

The two key conferences were Yalta (4–11 February 1945) and Potsdam (17 July – 2 August 1945). At Yalta, the Big Three agreed in principle on post-war Germany’s occupation zones, free elections in liberated Eastern Europe, and Soviet entry into the war against Japan. At Potsdam, a much cooler atmosphere prevailed: Truman had replaced Roosevelt, the USA had tested its first atomic bomb, and Stalin’s creation of a Soviet-dominated buffer in Eastern Europe was already apparent.

The Yalta Conference February 1945

The Yalta Conference brought together the three Allied leaders while Germany’s defeat was still weeks away. Yalta produced agreements on paper that were later contested in practice. Germany would be divided into four occupation zones, shared between the USA, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union. Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, would be similarly divided. Stalin committed to allow “free and unfettered elections” in Poland and other liberated states, a pledge that carried very different meanings in Washington and Moscow.

Roosevelt was already seriously ill at Yalta and died on 12 April 1945, before the war ended. His approach had been to seek Soviet co-operation through engagement — he believed that if the USSR was treated as a legitimate great power, it would act responsibly in the post-war order. Critics later argued he was too accommodating; supporters pointed out that the Red Army was already in Eastern Europe and the USA needed Soviet participation in the Pacific war.

The Potsdam Conference July–August 1945

By the time the three powers met at Potsdam, the context had changed dramatically. Germany had surrendered on 8 May 1945 (VE Day). Roosevelt had been replaced by Harry S. Truman, who was less inclined to accommodate Stalin. At Potsdam, Truman informed Stalin that the USA had “a new weapon of unusual destructive force” — the atomic bomb, tested successfully at Alamogordo on 16 July 1945. Stalin already knew about the Manhattan Project through espionage but gave no obvious reaction.

The Potsdam agreements confirmed the division of Germany and established the principle of reparations in kind from each zone. The Western powers grew increasingly concerned about Soviet actions in their occupation zone. Disputes about the German-Polish border, the treatment of German civilians expelled from Eastern Europe, and the nature of the governments being installed in Poland and Romania generated tensions that were not resolved before the conference ended.

Between 1945 and 1948, the Soviet Union systematically consolidated communist control across Eastern Europe. In Poland, Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria, coalition governments that included non-communist parties were progressively dismantled — a process that Hungarian communist leader Mátyás Rákosi described as “salami tactics” — slicing away the opposition one piece at a time. The most dramatic example was Czechoslovakia, where a communist coup in February 1948 removed the last non-communist government in Eastern Europe.

On 5 March 1946, Winston Churchill delivered his famous speech at Fulton, Missouri, warning that “an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.” Churchill was no longer Prime Minister — he had lost the British general election in July 1945, replaced by Clement Attlee at Potsdam — but his speech captured the growing anxiety in the West about Soviet intentions. The Iron Curtain metaphor became the defining image of the emerging Cold War division.

Two Perspectives on Responsibility

Historians have long debated which side bears more responsibility for the breakdown of wartime co-operation. The orthodox, or traditional, view — dominant in Western scholarship from the late 1940s to the early 1960s — placed primary responsibility on Soviet expansionism. On this reading, Stalin pursued a calculated policy of extending Soviet power westward, breaking the Yalta pledges on free elections and using salami tactics to install puppet governments. The Western powers were reacting defensively to Soviet aggression.

The revisionist view, which emerged strongly from American scholarship in the 1960s, shifted the emphasis. Historians associated with this school argued that US atomic diplomacy — the possession and use of the atomic bomb — was a deliberate attempt to intimidate the Soviet Union. American economic expansion through aid programmes and trade agreements was characterised as “dollar imperialism.” The USA, on this reading, was not simply reacting but actively projecting power. It is worth noting that the Soviet Union had lost approximately 27 million people in the Second World War; Soviet leaders had security concerns that were genuine, not simply pretextual, whatever one concludes about the methods used to address them. The examiner notes for this unit specifically ask for both views to be treated as “live historical positions, not as the textbook version versus heresy.”

Key Fact

The orthodox view holds that Soviet expansionism and the breaking of Yalta pledges drove the Cold War. The revisionist view holds that American atomic diplomacy and economic power projection were equally or more responsible. Post-revisionist historians (such as John Lewis Gaddis in later work) sought a middle ground, recognising both sides acted from genuine security fears in a system that generated misperception and mistrust.

The February 1948 communist coup in Czechoslovakia was a turning point in Western opinion. Czechoslovakia had maintained a coalition government and relatively free press longer than other Eastern European countries; its forcible takeover shocked Western publics and governments. Within weeks, the Western powers began serious discussions about a mutual defence pact that would become NATO in April 1949. The Czech coup also gave impetus to the Berlin Blockade crisis later in 1948, as Soviet pressure on Western access to Berlin further hardened the division of Europe into two camps.
exam_tip_html: For questions on Yalta and Potsdam, know the key differences between the two conferences: the change of US leadership (Roosevelt to Truman), the atomic bomb test, and the much cooler atmosphere at Potsdam. Do not conflate the two conferences. For Cold War origins questions, the orthodox vs. revisionist debate is directly examinable — treat both as legitimate historical positions. Note that Czechoslovakia initially wanted to accept Marshall Aid but was vetoed by Stalin: this fact is useful evidence for the Soviet control argument, and appears in the plan for the next lesson.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • At Yalta (February 1945) the Big Three agreed on Germany’s occupation zones and free elections in Eastern Europe; at Potsdam (July–August 1945) a cooler atmosphere prevailed as Truman replaced Roosevelt and Soviet control of Eastern Europe was already tightening.
  • Between 1945 and 1948, Soviet “salami tactics” dismantled non-communist governments across Eastern Europe, culminating in the Czech coup of February 1948; Churchill’s March 1946 “Iron Curtain” speech named the emerging division.
  • Historians are divided on responsibility: the orthodox view blames Soviet expansionism; the revisionist view emphasises US atomic diplomacy and economic power projection; the examiner expects both positions to be treated as legitimate.

practice_questions.text: Outline two agreements made at the Yalta Conference in February 1945.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each agreement scores 1 mark for identification and 1 for detail. Examples: Germany would be divided into four occupation zones (1) shared between the USA, Britain, France, and the USSR (1); Stalin pledged to hold free and unfettered elections in liberated Eastern European countries (1), including Poland (1); the Soviet Union agreed to enter the war against Japan (1) after Germany's defeat (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Potsdam Conference of July-August 1945 was more tense than the Yalta Conference.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed — Truman had replaced Roosevelt and was far less inclined to accommodate Stalin; the successful test of the atomic bomb gave the USA a new source of leverage and created new suspicion. Each with specific evidence and causal analysis. Secure: Both explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained, one named. Emerging: General reference to tension without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Soviet 'salami tactics' in Eastern Europe 1945-1948.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature plus 1 for detail. Feature 1: Coalition governments were progressively dismantled (1); non-communist parties and politicians were removed from power one at a time (1). Feature 2: The process culminated in a communist coup in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 (1); this was the last non-communist government in Eastern Europe to be removed (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why historians disagree about which side was more responsible for the origins of the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that orthodox historians emphasise Soviet expansionism and broken Yalta pledges (using evidence such as salami tactics, Czech coup); revisionist historians emphasise US atomic diplomacy and dollar imperialism (using evidence such as atomic bomb use, Marshall Plan as economic pressure); post-revisionist historians acknowledge genuine security fears on both sides leading to misperception. Connects the different evidence bases to show why historians reach different conclusions. Secure: Two or more perspectives explained with evidence. Developing: One perspective explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about disagreement without content.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of who was responsible for the Cold War. Interpretation A (orthodox view) argues Soviet expansionism and broken Yalta pledges drove the breakdown. Interpretation B (revisionist view) argues US atomic diplomacy and economic power projection were equally or more responsible. How far do these interpretations differ and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (who is the primary actor, what evidence each selects); uses own knowledge (salami tactics vs. atomic bomb, Yalta pledges vs. Marshall Plan context) to support both; explains reasons for disagreement (Cold War era writing, access to archives, political context). Secure: Explains differences with relevant evidence. Developing: Notes differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was Soviet policy in Eastern Europe the main cause of the Cold War by 1948? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Soviet actions (salami tactics, Czech coup, broken Yalta pledges) against US actions (atomic bomb, Truman's harder line at Potsdam, dollar diplomacy); engages with named schools (orthodox, revisionist, post-revisionist); reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: Clear argument addressing Soviet policy and at least one alternative cause with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument, may focus entirely on Soviet actions or entirely on the USA. Emerging: Descriptive account. SPaG: 5 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: Which leader replaced Roosevelt at the Potsdam Conference in July 1945?
What phrase did Churchill use in his March 1946 speech to describe the division of Europe?
Soviet tactics of gradually eliminating non-communist parties from coalition governments was called _____ tactics.
The Yalta Conference took place in _____ 1945.
Match each figure to their role at or around these conferences.
right: British PM who replaced Churchill at Potsdam

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Yalta Conference and who attended?
What happened at Yalta regarding Eastern Europe?
flashcard_questions.a: Stalin pledged free and unfettered elections in liberated Eastern European states including Poland

flashcard_questions.q: What changed between Yalta and Potsdam?
flashcard_questions.a: Roosevelt died; Truman replaced him; the atomic bomb was tested; Soviet control of Eastern Europe was tightening
Gradually eliminating non-communist parties from coalition governments, one slice at a time

flashcard_questions.q: When and where did Churchill give his 'Iron Curtain' speech?
What happened in Czechoslovakia in February 1948?
flashcard_questions.a: A communist coup removed the last non-communist government in Eastern Europe

flashcard_questions.q: What is the orthodox view of Cold War origins?
flashcard_questions.a: Soviet expansionism and broken Yalta pledges drove the breakdown of co-operation

flashcard_questions.q: What is the revisionist view of Cold War origins?
flashcard_questions.a: US atomic diplomacy and economic power projection were equally or more responsible

flashcard_questions.q: What was decided about Germany at Yalta and confirmed at Potsdam?
flashcard_questions.a: Germany and Berlin would be divided into four occupation zones among the USA, Britain, France, and the USSR

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how many people did the Soviet Union lose in the Second World War?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 27 million — a key context for understanding Soviet security demands after 1945

glossary_terms.definition: The wartime conference in the Crimea (February 1945) attended by Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin, at which the Allies discussed the post-war division of Germany and free elections in Eastern Europe.

The conference near Berlin (July-August 1945) at which the USA, Britain, and the USSR negotiated the post-war settlement for Germany; marked by increased tension between the West and the Soviet Union.
The gradual process by which Soviet-aligned communist parties took exclusive control of Eastern European governments between 1945 and 1948, eliminating non-communist partners one at a time.
Churchill's phrase, used in his March 1946 Fulton speech, describing the line dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from Western Europe.
